newsitem.title: JAPAN: N.Korea's Kim Jong-il has crown within his grasp.
newsitem.headline: N.Korea's Kim Jong-il has crown within his grasp.

text.p: North Korean strongman Kim Jong-il, once dismissed as unlikely to last the distance, is within a month of an anniversary that will position him to formally become leader of the communist nation.

As the third anniversary approaches of the death of his father on July 8, 1994, Kim's survival against daunting odds has set off a major reassessment in the West of his leadership qualities and the support he enjoys in his homeland.

North Korean sources indicated that shortly after the anniversary, which marks the end of the traditional mourning period, Kim would take on the trappings of power by assuming the titles of general secretary of the ruling Workers' Party and state president, positions held by his father, the "Great Leader" Kim Il-sung.
They said there would be no grand announcement on July 8 -- that would be insensitive -- but two or three months later the 55-year-old Kim was likely to be anointed.

Once garishly portrayed as a brandy-swilling paranoid playboy interested only in films, Kim is now seen as a power in his own right who can boast he has almost weathered the succession storm and held his nation together.
There have been tests aplenty along the way.

How to fill the shoes of the man who founded your nation; carry out communism's first dynastic succession; keep your enemies at bay; your people quiet; convince the world to keep talking to you; and cope with a famine caused by record floods.

Although in most western eyes, North Korea on the surface remains the last great ogre of the communist world -- sullen, isolated, impenetrable and running against the tide of history -- Kim can claim at least partial success in all tests,

"The image of Kim Jong-il as the leader of a terrorist state has been fading away in the past three years," said Noriyuki Suzuki, chief analyst at Radiopress, a Tokyo-based agency that monitors North Korea's official media.
"He is now seen as a realist and tough negotiator who has skillfully controlled the country since his father's death."
But with the formal crown of leadership almost in his grasp, Kim over the next month or so could face his biggest tests.
"If there is going to be a leadership challenge -- and there are no signs of one -- then it must come in the weeks before Kim is formally anointed," one North Korea watcher said.

International aid agencies also forecast that from mid-June, already famine-like food shortages were likely to strike hardest while the population anxiously awaits the results of the first crops planted without flood interference in two years.
"You can't completely rule out the possibility of North Korea being hit by floods again this year," Suzuki said.
"If that happens, the whole succession process gets bogged down and Kim Jong-il will be forced to wait much longer to formally succeed his father," he said.
"The food situation remains the key to the future of Kim Jong-il."

Suzuki and some other North Korea watchers speculate that the signal of a final push by Kim for formal power would be a drastic reshuffle of the cabinet and posts in the ruling Workers' Party in the coming weeks.
Two months ago, Kim made his move to secure his key power base in the military by promoting more than 120 young officers to generals.
A senior Western diplomat said the promotions were the final proof that Kim was in sole charge of the country, and not some puppet, directed by elderly comrades of his father.
"No-one now questions that he is in charge and calling the shots," the diplomat said.

Although there have been many setbacks along the way, notably the defection earlier this year of North Korea's ideology chief, Kim has proved his harshest critics wrong in managing to keep his country afloat.
His achievements have included opening a tenuous dialogue with the United States that could lead to Korean Peninsula peace talks and a landmark nuclear deal with Washington.

Under the $4.5 billion deal, Washington promised two light-water reactors generating 1,000 megawatts of power each by around 2003 if Pyongyang freezes and ultimately dismantles its existing nuclear programme.
"Is the glass half empty or half full? one Korean analyst asked in reviewing the past three years. "From North Korea's point of view, I'd say it is half full."
